1.pericope_label: Peter and John at the hour of prayer

schools.summary: Chrysostom observes that we find these two everywhere in great harmony, Peter beckoning to John at the supper, the two coming together to the sepulchre, Peter asking afterwards what this man should do. He notes that the writer passes over the other miracles and records the one by which all were put in commotion, and that the apostles did not come purposely, being so clear of ambition and so closely imitating their Master; they went up to the temple not because they still lived as Jews but for expediency, and the sign both confirmed the converts and drew over the rest. Of the man he says the disease lay in his nature and baffled the art of medicine, that the most obstinate diseases are those born with a man, and that the calamity was such that he could not provide his own sustenance; he had been lame forty years and nobody in all that time had cured him, so that he was conspicuous both from the place and from his malady.

Cyril sets the healing in the same power of the Holy Ghost by which Peter had stood with the Eleven and captured three thousand souls in the spiritual net of his words. In that same power, he says, Peter and John went up into the temple at the hour of prayer, which was the ninth hour, and in the name of Jesus healed the man at the Beautiful gate who had been lame from his mother's womb for forty years, that the word might be fulfilled, then shall the lame man leap as an hart.

Gill says the two were intimate companions and great lovers of each other, thought by some to have been together in the high priest's palace at the trial, and holds that they went up not to attend the daily sacrifice, which was abolished by the sacrifice of Christ, but to the duty of prayer, which was still in force, and that they might have opportunity of preaching Christ where a body of people was gathered. Calvin notes that Luke recites one miracle out of many for example's sake and gathers all the circumstances that set it forth: a dislocated limb or an injury by accident might have been more easily cured, but a defect of nature could not; that the man was carried shows it was no light halting but that he lay as if his legs were dead; that he asked alms daily made him the better known to all the people; and that he walked in the temple at the hour of prayer spread the fame of it. Calvin will not put the visit down to the rite of the law, thinking it likelier the two went up for the better opportunity of spreading the gospel; and he refuses to let the verse be made a licence for joining in superstitious worship, since God himself had appointed the morning and evening sacrifice, so that men who came into a house consecrated to God and called on the God of Israel polluted themselves in nothing. He divides the day into four parts, takes the ninth for the last of them, and draws from that the probable conjecture that this was the hour of the evening sacrifice; and he adds that the appointed hours show the Church cannot be without some settled discipline.

Henry supposes that Peter and John presided over the society Luke was associated with, which is why he records what they said and did so particularly. He notices that each of the two had a brother among the twelve with whom he had been coupled when they were sent out, yet they are now knit more closely to each other than to their own kin, there being a friend that sticks closer than a brother; and he offers a conjecture for it, that John, a disciple made up of love, was more compassionate to Peter upon his fall and more solicitous to restore him in the spirit of meekness than any of the rest, so that Christ's favourite becoming his bosom friend was itself good evidence of Peter's acceptance with God upon his repentance. Of the place he says it is good to go up to the temple and comfortable to go up together, the best society being society in worshipping God; of the hour, that time and place are necessary circumstances of every action and must be settled as is most convenient for edification, and that it is of use for private Christians to have their hours of prayer, not to bind conscience but to remind it. Of the man he observes that such piteous cases are designed to show us what we all are by nature spiritually, without strength, lame from our birth, unable to walk in God's service.

Clarke argues that the words rendered together should be rendered at that time, marking that this happened near the events at the close of the previous chapter. He sets out the three hours of prayer, the third answering to nine in the morning, the sixth to noon and the ninth to three in the afternoon, reports the rabbinic ascription of the three to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and prefers Tanchum's division, that men should pray when the sun rises, when it gains the meridian and when it sets — adding that he should be glad to know every Christian observed the rule, since he who conscientiously keeps these three stated times will infallibly grow in grace. Wesley explains that the twelve hours ran from sunrise to sunset and were therefore of unequal length as the days lengthened or shortened, the third hour being the middle space between sunrise and noon; the chief hours of prayer were the third and the ninth, when the morning and evening sacrifices were offered and incense, an emblem of prayer, was burnt on the golden altar.

Barnes notes that the disciples resorted daily to the temple, that whether they joined in its sacrifices is not said though not improbable, and that they came only slowly to the conclusion that they were to leave it; the place meant is not the edifice properly so called but the court where prayer was accustomed to be made. He adds a point about the narrative itself, that Luke descends to particulars where an impostor would have been content with a general claim of many wonders, which is proof that the writers did not intend to deceive. Ellicott lays out the whole record of the friendship — partners as fishermen, sharers in looking for the consolation of Israel, sent together to prepare the passover, John taking Peter into the high priest's palace and not estranged from him by the denials, Peter turning to John for comfort after his fall — and disposes of Renan's notion that the fourth Gospel was written to exalt its author at Peter's expense, which may take its place among the morbid imaginations of inventive interpretation. He identifies the hour as three in the afternoon, that of the evening sacrifice, traces the practice of praying three times a day back through Daniel to David, and observes that both the three hours and the seven of the more devout passed into the usage of the Christian Church, the seven becoming the canonical hours of Western Christendom. Robertson catches the imperfect, that they were ascending the terraces to the temple courts, and notes that Peter and John, like Paul after them, kept up the Jewish worship without treating it as a means of sacramental redemption.
