why they went up to the temple

2.pericope_label: The lame man at the Beautiful gate

schools.summary: Gill notes that the lameness came neither from disease nor from a fall but from a defect in nature in one limb or more, which made the miracle that followed the more extraordinary; that the man looked at the two though they were strangers to him, concluding from their entering the temple at that hour that they were Israelites; and that when Peter fastened his eyes on him he was doubtless under an uncommon impulse of the Spirit of God. Of the man's response Gill says only that he not merely attended to them in his mind but directed his eyes toward them and looked wistly. Calvin raises the question the moment suggests, whether the apostles could work miracles as often as they pleased, and answers that they were ministers of God's power in such sort that they attempted nothing of their own will or motion, but that the Lord wrought by them when he knew it expedient — which is why they healed one man and not all; they had the Spirit for their guide in this as in other things, and the steadfast looking was itself a peculiar motion of the Spirit, without which Peter could not have spoken so surely of the miracle. Calvin also finds in the beggar an example of prayer: God restored him contrary to his expectation, and what was given he had never dared to ask, so that God often prevents us and shows himself to those who do not seek him — yet this is no occasion of slothfulness, since we are commanded to pray and must not omit our part.

Clarke observes that the case must have been notorious both from the long standing of the infirmity and from the man's daily exposure in so public a place, and that Luke marks these circumstances to show the greatness and incontestable nature of the miracle. On the gate he quotes Josephus, that the temple had nine gates covered with gold and silver, but that one outside the holy house, of Corinthian brass, greatly excelled them, its height fifty cubits and its doors forty, adorned with much richer and thicker plates; this was probably the gate meant, though he grants the text of Josephus is by no means clear. Of the command to look he says Peter wished to engage the man's attention that he might see what was done to produce the cure, and probably took the occasion to direct his faith to Jesus Christ, the two apostles having felt themselves suddenly drawn by the Holy Spirit to pronounce the healing name. Wesley assigns the gate to Herod the Great, setting it between the court of the Gentiles and that of Israel, thirty cubits high and fifteen broad, made of Corinthian brass and more pompous in its workmanship and splendour than those overlaid with silver and gold.

Barnes takes the lifelong lameness as proof that there was no deception, since the man had always been lame, had to be carried, and was well known to those who used that entrance. He explains the begging from a world with neither hospitals nor alms-houses, where the poor depended on charity and had to be placed where many would see them, at the gates of rich men or beside the highway; the temple entrance was the most favourable of all, since multitudes passed and men going up for religion give more freely, the Pharisees particularly, who wanted their charity seen. He adds that the custom of placing the poor at the gates of temples is recorded by Martial among the Romans and was long observed in Christian churches. On the gate he inclines to the eastern entrance called Susan, since the sequel places the crowd at Solomon's porch. Of the fixed gaze he notes that the word means to look with intent attention, that it is one of this writer's peculiar words, used by no other in the New Testament save Paul twice, and that the command to look was meant to fix the man's attention on the source of the cure. Ellicott finds the record of duration characteristic of this writer and thinks the minuteness of the narrative suggests the informant may have been the cripple himself; the approaches of the temple, like those of modern mosques, were thronged with the blind and the lame. He offers two candidates for the gate with their traditions — Nicanor, so called on one account because the hand of the great enemy of Judah had been nailed to it as a trophy, and the Susa gate, named for the old connection between Judah and Persia and so massive that twenty men were needed to open or shut it. He makes the gaze mutual: Peter read character in the man's face and discerned faith to be healed, while the man was to read in their pitying looks not only the wish to heal but the power to do it. Robertson catches the tenses, that Peter fixed his eyes and invited the man to look, and that the man held his own on them with great eagerness, taking the invitation for the promise of a large gift.

debates.question: Which gate of the temple was the Beautiful gate?

positions.position: probably the eastern entrance called Susan, since the crowd afterwards gathers at Solomon's porch
either the Nicanor gate or the Susa gate, no gate of this name being mentioned by any other writer
the Corinthian gate described by Josephus, fifty cubits high, added by Herod between the court of the Gentiles and that of Israel

outliers.note: uses the fixed gaze to answer a larger question, whether the apostles could work miracles at will: they attempted nothing of their own motion, which is why one man was healed and not all

themes: why the case could not be faked

6.pericope_label: Silver and gold have I none

schools.summary: Gill takes the poverty strictly, that they had no coin of either metal about them and perhaps none of their own anywhere, only what was brought and put into their hands as a common stock for the whole church; and he notes that no money might be carried in a purse into the temple at all, though it might be carried in the hand for the offerings or for the poor, or the man would not have lain there for alms. Calvin turns the confession into a rule of charity: Peter truly excuses himself for wanting the help required and declares that he would willingly relieve the man's poverty if he could, as every man ought to consider what the Lord has given him, since whatever store God bestows is meant as an instrument for exercising love. He grants that the opening looks like a trick of mockery, Peter speaking of his poverty after raising so rare a hope, but the comparison makes the miracle the greater. Of the name Calvin is careful on two sides: there is no magical force in the sounding or pronouncing of the word, as the Jews dote about the name Jehovah, and Peter meant only to declare himself a minister and Christ the author of the miracle; while the added epithet is deliberate, since Nazareth was the term of contempt, and Peter of set purpose named the very Jesus they had crucified, whose name was despised and to most detestable, as the Messiah promised of God. He also draws the whole into a type of our spiritual restoring, since as the word laid hold on by faith restored the cripple, so the Lord pierces into our souls by the word. Calvin adds a fierce aside on the papal ceremony of the two stone cells, where the newly created pope, asked for alms in Peter's own words, casts crosses in the air with his fingers and is then carried to the cell where the bags of money are while his attendants cry that he has dispersed and given to the poor; Satan reigns, he says, where the Word of God is so manifestly mocked.

Clarke observes that though it was customary for all who entered the temple to carry some money, the apostles were so poor that they had nothing to give either to the treasury or to the distressed; and he notes that the popish writers, dexterous as they are at forming analogies between Peter and the pope, have attempted none here, even Calmet passing the saying by. He tells the story of Thomas Aquinas entering the chamber of Innocent the Fourth while large sums were counted, and the pope saying, you see the Church is no longer in an age when she can say, silver and gold have I none — to which the angelical doctor replied, true, holy father, nor can she now say to the lame man, rise up and walk. Clarke adds the remark that though the saints of that church work no miracles alive they work many when dead, and that it is the attestation of such posthumous miracles that leads to canonisation. Wesley puts the same point in two lines: how unlike his supposed successor, and can the bishop of Rome either say or do the same?

Barnes reads the answer as a refusal made so as to show willingness, and glosses the next phrase as such as is in my power, without any suggestion that Peter had originated it, since he immediately adds that the power was derived from the Lord Jesus. On the name he explains that the phrase means by his authority, or in virtue of power derived from him, and finds in it a radical difference between the Lord's miracles and the apostles': Christ wrought in his own name and by his own power, claiming dominion over disease and death, whereas the apostles never attempted a miracle by their own power, which alone shows that there was a difference in kind between Christ and all other teachers. He notes too the form of the command, that the man was told to do the thing at once rather than to attempt it or to wait for strength — precisely, he says, as a sinner is commanded to repent and believe rather than merely to use means. Ellicott presses the difficulty that the apostles were by then stewards of the sums the community had laid at their feet, so that either they had none with them, or as almoners they held themselves bound to distribute what was given in trust only to members of the society; obeying their Master's command, they had no money of their own, but they could give more than money. He makes the trust behind the words partly faith in their Master's promise and partly the memory of powers already exercised, and observes that the Name can hardly have been new to the beggar, since a fellow at that gate had received his sight at Siloam and the healing at Bethesda can scarcely have been unknown to a sufferer from a like infirmity — what made the call a test of faith being that a few weeks earlier that Name had stood on the superscription of a cross. Robertson notes that the healing power is in that name and that Peter says so, and that the command to walk is inchoative, begin walking and keep on — but the beggar does not budge, knowing that he cannot.

debates.question: How could men who administered the church's common fund say they had no silver or gold?

positions.position: they had none with them, or as almoners were bound to distribute what was held in trust only to members of the society; of their own they had nothing
they had none at all of their own, and no money might in any case be carried in a purse into the temple

outliers.note: guards the name from both sides at once — no magical force in the syllables, as the Jews dote about the name Jehovah, and no credit to the minister, since Peter names the despised Jesus of Nazareth precisely as the promised Messiah

themes: what the poverty of the apostles amounted to
the verse turned against the papacy

schools.summary: Gill notes that Peter took the man by the right hand in imitation of Christ, whom he had often seen use the same action on such occasions, and that the man leaped up from the bed or couch or ground on which he lay.

Clarke makes the timing the proof: the suddenness of the cure was the proof of the miracle, and the walking and leaping were its evidences. He distinguishes the three acts that followed — he walked in obedience to the command to rise up and walk, he leaped to try the strength of his limbs and to be convinced of the reality of the cure, and he praised God as a testimony of the gratitude he felt; and in all this, Clarke says, the words of the prophet were now fulfilled in the most literal manner, that the lame man shall leap as an hart.

Barnes reads the taking of the hand as an offer of aid, an indication that Peter was sincere, and an inducement to the man to make an effort, and turns it into an illustration of God's manner in commanding men to repent and believe, since he does not leave them alone but extends help and aids their efforts. That strength was imparted at once to feet lame from birth he takes for full and clear proof of miraculous power. He finds a further proof in the walking itself, since walking is a skill acquired by long practice and children learn it slowly — he instances Caspar Hauser, lately discovered in a German city, who had been confined from childhood and could only stumble awkwardly when released — so that a man who walked at once was clearly healed by more than the giving of strength. Of the praise Barnes notes that it went to God without prompting and without a word of thanks to Peter and John, who had not pretended to restore him in their own name, and that a renewed sinner does the same, ascribing the whole to God though he feels regard for the ministry by which the blessing came. Ellicott would render the first word as soles rather than feet, and observes that this term and the ankle bones alike are more or less technical, as is the verb rendered received strength, which means literally that they were consolidated, the flaccid tissues and muscles made firm and vigorous; the precision, he says, is characteristic of a medical historian. He traces the order of movements — first the upward leap in the new consciousness of power, then the successful effort to stand for the first time in his life, then the beginning of walking step by step, and at last the two motions alternating, ordinary walking broken by the leaps of an exuberant joy — noting that the verb is a compound of the one the Greek version uses in the promise that the lame shall leap as an hart, and that the court he entered would at the hour of the evening sacrifice have been full of worshippers. Robertson puts the practical fact more bluntly, that Peter had to pull the man up onto his feet before he would try to walk, and notes that he kept leaping repeatedly and came into the temple rehearsing all three new exercises together.

outliers.note: finds a second miracle inside the first, since walking is a skill learned slowly — a man lame from birth who walked at once had been given more than strength

themes: the hand offered before the strength came
the medical precision of the description

9.pericope_label: The people run to Solomon's porch

schools.summary: Gill points out that the man had been brought there daily and had sat asking alms for years, so that he was thoroughly known, and that the people now staring at him had passed him minutes before in his old condition; it was, he says, a clear and indisputable point with them. Calvin grants a double fruit in what follows, since the healed man acknowledges and sets forth the benefit of God while the people are moved and the fame spreads and many come to see; but he insists that being filled with wondering describes only a preparation, which a fuller progress had afterwards to follow. Of itself the amazement rather astonished the people than brought them to God, and it was the foundation of a building still to come. From this he draws a rule: miracles by themselves breed nothing but a confused astonishment, and though God calls us to himself by showing his goodness and power in them, such is the weakness of our nature that we stumble or faint in the midway until doctrine helps us. Where none reproves it, he adds, the abuse of miracles has bred the superstitious worship of saints, since a man who acknowledges the power of God in a miracle is easily persuaded by Satan that he owes divine honour to the man who wrought it — and the same would have befallen these Jews in their amazement had not Peter's sermon called them back into the right way. Wonder must therefore be joined to teaching, and the one never separated from the other. Calvin adds a note on the porch itself, that the old temple was pulled down but Zerubbabel and Ezra imitated it as nearly as they could contrive, and that though Herod renewed the building and made it far more gorgeous, all that vain cost had not blotted the remembrance of Solomon out of the people's hearts.

Clarke presses the publicity, that the miracle was wrought in the most public manner and in the most public place, and in a place where the best judgment could be formed of it, since as it was a divine operation the priests were the proper persons to judge, and it was wrought under their notice. Of the man's clinging to his benefactors he says it was the strongest affection for the instruments by which the divine influence had been conveyed to his diseased body.

Barnes lists the particulars as things no imposture could satisfy: the man had been afflicted from a child and was by now forty; had he been feigning, he could hardly have escaped detection all that while in so public a place; the apostles had no hand in placing him there and had never seen him, so there was no room for collusion; the man himself was convinced, and so were the people, who had had every opportunity of knowing his condition. Nor were these friends of Jesus, but men lately busy putting him to death. Compare this miracle in these particulars, Barnes says, with the pretended miracles alleged in defence of other systems of religion, and there is every appearance of sincerity and truth here and every mark of imposition there. Ellicott would render the verb as recognised, they recognised him that it was he, and describes the portico as standing outside the temple on the east, a double row of Corinthian columns some thirty-seven feet high, which took its name from having been built in part, when the temple was raised again under Zerubbabel, from fragments of the older edifice; the people afterwards pressed Herod Agrippa to pull it down and rebuild it, but he shrank from the cost. Like the porticoes of Greek cities it was a favourite resort, facing the morning sun in winter. He adds what the two disciples must have remembered, that here the people had once taken up stones against Jesus for saying he was one with the Father, and here they were now to hear his name preached as Holy and Just. Robertson catches the tense, that they were beginning to perceive who it was, and notes that the word for porch is the one behind the name Stoic, that the portico stood on the east of the court of the Gentiles and was so called from being built on a remnant of the ancient foundations, and that Jesus had once taught there.

outliers.note: treats the crowd's amazement as raw material rather than result: miracles of themselves breed only a confused astonishment, and where no teaching follows the same wonder has bred the worship of saints

12.pericope_label: Why look ye so earnestly on us?

schools.summary: Chrysostom finds greater freedom of speech in this address than in the earlier one, not because Peter had been afraid before but because the hearers that day were jesters and scoffers who would not have borne it and had to be secured by an opening request for attention. Here no such management was needed, since the miracle had roused everybody and they were full of fear and amazement; so the speaker begins elsewhere, by rejecting the glory to be had from them — nothing being so advantageous, or so likely to pacify hearers, as to say nothing honourable about oneself and to obviate all surmise of wishing to. In truth, he adds, they increased their glory the more by despising glory and by showing that what had happened was no human act but a divine work, in which their part was to join the beholders in admiration rather than to receive it from them. He sets the same modesty in a longer line, since Daniel disclaimed any wisdom of his own, Joseph asked whether interpretations did not belong to God, and David ascribed the lion and the bear to the name of the Lord; and Peter presses himself on the fathers of old lest he seem to introduce a new doctrine.

Gill notes that Peter saw the people running to them and looking wistly and wondering at what was done. Calvin observes that the reproof does not fall on their wondering, which was altogether profitable and worthy of praise, but on their wickedly ascribing to men the praise due to the work of God: it is to be amazed evilly when our minds stay in men. He grants that no one denies power to come from God; the trouble is that men confess it in a word and then take from God his right to adorn the creature with what they have taken, so that the power of God is placed in the saints and shut up in a stone or a stock of wood as soon as the image is consecrated. Even granting they do not offend in that first article, they think they have satisfied God by leaving him the power while assigning the miracles to the godliness of saints — a childish subterfuge, since men would not run to the saints for rain or fair weather or health unless they supposed some merit had earned the privilege. Calvin adds a note on method: because men are inclined to nothing more than to fall from God to the creatures, it is expedient to prevent the vice in time, and if the people were forbidden to look to the apostles, much more does the Spirit draw us from calling on every petty saint.

Henry sets out three things Peter saw and used: a crowd in the temple, where a wisdom more excellent than Solomon's might be heard; a people wondering, which was ground broken up and ready for the seed; and a people on the point of adoring him, which made him step in at once, as Paul did at Lystra. He asks with Peter why they should marvel at this, since it was no more than Christ had done many a time and they had not been affected by it — Lazarus had lately been raised, and Christ himself had lately risen. He presses the point through a series of denials: not by any might of their own, since they had no skill in physic and no virtue in their word; not by any merit, since Peter was a sinful man and Judas, who had no holiness at all, wrought miracles in Christ's name — and draws the rule that the instruments of God's favour must be respected but never idolized, and that useful men must see to it that they be very humble, every crown being cast at the feet of Christ.

Clarke glosses the first term as miraculous energy and the second as religious attachment to the worship of God, and notes that some copies read power for holiness, though the received word appears to be the true one; the sense is, do not think we have wrought this by any power of our own, or that any supereminent piety in us induced God to honour us by enabling us to work it. Wesley says only that Peter answered the people, who were running together and inquiring into the circumstances of the fact.

Barnes explains that the word answered does not imply that a question had been asked but marks an occasion offered for remarks, and is careful about what is reproved: not the wondering, which was proper, but the fixing of their eyes on the two men as if these were the authors of the cure — the Jews being sufficiently acquainted with miracles to interpret them and to know whence they proceeded. He observes that the opportunity to claim a reputation was open and was refused, and draws the rule that whatever success may attend ministers of the gospel, and however much the world may honour them, they should disclaim all power in themselves and ascribe it to the Lord Jesus. Ellicott points out that the pronoun stands emphatically first — why is it on us that ye gaze? — and would render the second noun as purity or devotion. The word refers, he says, to the popular theory of miracles, that God hears a man who is a worshipper of him; true enough in general, but Peter disclaims it here, since no purity of his own would have availed apart from the Name. Robertson notes that the people looked their amazement and Peter answered the look, the address by the covenant name of Israel being conciliatory, and that the participle gives the alleged reason rather than the true one.

outliers.note: turns the disclaimer into a standing argument against invoking the saints, since men who leave God the power while crediting the miracle to a saint's godliness have not honoured him at all

themes: why this sermon needs no preamble

13.pericope_label: The God of the fathers has glorified his Servant

schools.summary: Cyril puts the same divine title to a different use, arguing from it against the Samaritans, who receive the Law only and admit no prophets, so that a text from Ezekiel has no force with them: since God tells Moses in the Law itself that he is the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob, this must mean of those who have being and subsistence.

Gill says the old epithets are retained partly to distinguish this God from the gods of the Gentiles and partly to show regard to the God of Israel, the one true and living God, lest men preaching Christ be taken for setters forth of a strange God; and on the second title he takes Christ to be holy in both natures and the fountain of holiness to his people, and just both in his person and in the discharge of his office, the words having a particular regard to the innocence of his life against the unjust charges of his enemies. Calvin makes the title a rule against two misuses. God gave himself this designation to distinguish himself by a mark from idols, since we cannot comprehend him in his essence, which is unseen and infinite, and he uses means that agree with our capacity; the Turks boast that they worship the maker of heaven and earth, but vanish away before they come at heaven, and God kept his people within his covenant to preserve them from erroneous inventions. Nor may the phrase be stretched into a warrant for whatever worship the fathers used: Peter expressly reckons up Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, from whom true religion proceeded, whereas many later fathers grew out of kind and became unlike the first, so that the prophets had to say, walk not in the ways of your fathers. Calvin adds that Peter tacitly reminds them they were no better than other men without the only begotten Son, and that the comparison between Pilate and the accusers is drawn to strike them home, since men must be so stricken that, brought to know their guilt, they may earnestly fly to the remedy of pardon.

Clarke turns the title into an accusation: the God they called their own had acknowledged Jesus for his Son and wrought this miracle in his name, so that by honouring the man they slew he charged the guilt of that murder home upon them. Of the trial he says they renounced him as their king and denounced him to death as a malefactor when Pilate judged it proper and just to let him go — Pilate wished to act according to justice, and they acted contrary to justice and equity in all their forms. He takes the first title as a manifest reference to the Psalm which promises that God will not suffer his Holy One to see corruption, and finds the choice of Barabbas characteristic, since like cleaves to like and they were murderers themselves, preferring a murderer to the holy and righteous One of God. Wesley says the title was wisely introduced at the opening so that it might appear they taught no new religion inconsistent with Moses, and had no design of diverting regard from the God of Israel; and of the delivering up he adds that God had given Christ to them, and they ought to have received him as a most precious treasure and preserved him with all their power.

Barnes notes that it was important to show that the God who had done this was the God their fathers had acknowledged, and that they were not introducing the worship of another; the promise to Abraham that in his seed all families of the earth should be blessed makes the title especially apt. He traces the legal position of the trial: the first charge was blasphemy, on which the council condemned him without proof, and when Pilate would not take cognisance of it they charged sedition instead, so that neither was made out and in the eye of the law he stood innocent — which aggravates the crime, since they urged his death against the judgment of the man before whom they had arraigned him. The word just, he adds, is properly a legal term for one who stands upright in the view of the law. Ellicott hears in the divine title an echo of their Master's own teaching, since the same Name had been spoken in these precincts, not improbably in this very portico, as part of his proof that the dead rise — and is heard again in support of the apostles' witness that he himself had risen. He renders the next word as Servant rather than Son, the term being used throughout the later chapters of Isaiah for the servant of Jehovah and, as applied to Christ, peculiar to this book; it is therefore more distinctive than Son would have been and implies the Messianic interpretation of that prophetic language. Of the two titles that follow he observes that, startling as they sounded, they had been anticipated: the demoniacs used the first of Christ, the best manuscripts give Peter's own earlier confession in the same words, and Pilate with his wife had borne witness to him as Just; both words recur in the letters of the two apostles now preaching them, which is what three years of converse with such a Master had left behind. Robertson agrees that the word is Servant and not son at all, notes the emphatic pronouns, ye set against that one, and a man a murderer set against the Holy and Righteous One, the verb meaning granted as a favour.

debates.question: What does the word rendered Son mean here?

positions.position: Servant — the term used through the later chapters of Isaiah for the servant of Jehovah, and as applied to Christ peculiar to this book

outliers.note: refuses to let the appeal to the fathers become a general warrant for ancestral religion, since Peter names Abraham, Isaac and Jacob precisely, and many later fathers grew out of kind

themes: why the God of the fathers is named

15.pericope_label: The Prince of life, and faith in his name

schools.summary: Gill takes the life meant to be natural, spiritual and eternal at once, since Christ has life in himself, had such power over his own life as no man ever had, is the author of a spiritual resurrection from the death of sin to a life of grace, and has procured eternal life for his people; and he holds the death justly laid to them, since it was at their request and instigation and their earnest solicitation that Pilate condemned him. On the healing he says that neither the faith of the apostles nor the faith of the man had any causal influence on the cure, but was the way and means in which, they glorifying Christ, he was pleased to effect it. Calvin is struck by the repetition of the name, which he takes for a token of fervent affection: Peter beats the same thing in again and again because he is wholly given to setting forth the glory of Christ, such being our nature that Christ can never be so extolled that his honour remains whole to him. He notes that the phrase shows both the cause and the manner, since the power of Christ healed the cripple but did so by faith, and that faith cannot rise up unto God unless it be grounded in Christ, so that there is no right faith in God when we pass over this mean. Calvin thinks the question whose faith it was hardly worth standing on, since it may be referred as well to the man healed as to the apostles.

Clarke derives the word from the roots for beginning and leading: not only does all life proceed from Christ, but the life-giving influence of the religion now proclaimed came through him — he teaches the doctrine of life, leads the way men should walk, and has purchased the life enjoyed at the end of it. So the Jews, he says, preferred a son of death, a destroyer of life, to the Author and Procurer of life and immortality. Of the witness he observes that having performed a striking miracle in that name the apostles at once propose themselves as witnesses of the resurrection, the miracle being an unimpeachable proof of it. On the question whose faith healed the man he will not settle it: the apostles may have asked this power of the Father in the name of Christ, as they had been promised they might, or the faith may have been the man's, since in the moments when they bade him look at them they may have taught him what to believe, his mind being already prepared by what he had heard of the gift of tongues. Either way, Clarke says, faith was only the means of receiving, which the apostles attribute not to their own power or holiness but to Jesus Christ alone: faith always receives and never gives.

Barnes explains that the word properly denotes a leader or commander, rendered captain elsewhere; since a commander leads on to victory and is said to obtain it, the word comes to mean the cause or author of a thing, and author or giver would express the sense here, with the added implication of dominion over life. He notes the contrast with the man they preferred, a murderer who had destroyed life, so that the destroyer was demanded and the Author of life put to death. On the sentence that follows he explains that the name stands for the person, after the Hebrew manner, so that no efficacy is ascribed to the syllables but to the authority of the one who bears them; and he takes the word rendered perfect soundness, found nowhere else in the New Testament, to mean integrity of parts and freedom from defect. He decides for the apostles' faith rather than the beggar's, since there is no evidence the man believed at all, and finds in it a fulfilment of the promise that faith would remove mountains. That the apostles invited the crowd to examine the man in their presence he thinks conclusive against imposture, since a deceiver would not have exposed his case to inspection. Ellicott distinguishes the efficient cause from the condition of its working: the Name did not operate as a formula of incantation, but required faith in what it represented, in worker and receiver alike — and he carries the causation a step further back, since the faith in both was itself wrought by the power of Christ, the man being first a willing recipient of that faith spiritually and then in a state to receive the bodily restoration. Robertson quotes Bengel's phrase, the magnificent antithesis between asking for a murderer and killing the Prince of life, and traces the word from an adjective for what furnishes the first cause to a noun meaning the originator; the claim that all had seen the risen Christ is bold, he adds, and was never denied.

debates.question: Whose faith is meant — the apostles' or the lame man's?

positions.position: the apostles', since there is no evidence that the man believed at all
not to be settled: it may have been either, and faith in any case only receives and never gives
both, and the faith in each was itself wrought by the power of Christ

outliers.note: denies that faith of either kind had any causal influence on the cure, allowing it only as the way and means in which Christ, being glorified, was pleased to effect it

themes: the Prince or Author of life

schools.summary: Gill says Peter calls them brethren because they were so according to the flesh, and to testify his cordial love and affection for them; and of the prophecies he notes that what God had before showed concerning the betraying of the Messiah, his sufferings and death, with their causes and circumstances, stood in the Scriptures of the Old Testament. Calvin explains the turn: since it was to be feared that men cast down with despair would refuse the doctrine altogether, Peter lifts them a little, and sermons must be so tempered that they profit the hearers, for where no hope of pardon is left the terror of punishment only hardens men — as David says, we fear the Lord when we perceive that he is easy to be pacified. Calvin will not let the plea be taken too simply, since hypocrisy lay hidden under this ignorance and an action is named from whichever ingredient abounds in it; his meaning is that they did it rather through error and a blind zeal than through determined wickedness. He answers the objection that the comparison with the rulers is unequal, since the scribes and priests were carried headlong with a wonderful madness while the people were pricked forward by a perverse zeal for the law and incensed by their rulers: they were not all of one mind, many being like Paul, so that Peter speaks not of all the rulers but invites the curable among them to repentance. On the fulfilment he puts comfort and caution together: ignorance made them guilty, yet God brought to pass what he had determined, that Christ should redeem them by his death; our evils are turned by his counsel to another end than we intended, which is no excuse, since so far as in us lies we destroy ourselves by sinning.

Clarke calls the plea a tender and a necessary excuse, since if the whole had been done in absolute malice, with full knowledge of the person, no sin could be less pardonable; Peter foresaw that they might be tempted to despair of salvation and tells them their offence was extenuated by their ignorance of the person they had tormented and crucified. Had they been fully convinced that this was the Messiah they would never have crucified him — but, Clarke adds, they did not permit themselves to receive conviction on the subject. Of the fulfilment he says their ignorance and malice were overruled by the sovereign wisdom and power of God and became instruments of fulfilling his purpose, that Christ must suffer to make an atonement for the sin of the world; all the prophets declared it, some in express terms and others indirectly and by symbols, since the whole Mosaic dispensation referred to Christ. Wesley calls the address a word full of courtesy and compassion, spoken to their heart, and finds a second delicacy in the phrase about the rulers, since Peter does not say our rulers but yours — the Jewish dispensation having ceased at the death of Christ, and with it the authority of its officers; and of God he says only that he, who was not ignorant, permitted what he had foretold, to bring good out of it.

Barnes finds the verse a remarkable instance of tenderness in appealing to sinners, since after proving a crime so enormous Peter still addresses them as of the same nation and hope, which shows he was not setting himself up as more holy by nature; men are melted to contrition, he says, not by reproaches but by love. He denies that the plea makes them innocent; the offence was mitigated but not removed, since they had demanded the death of a man declared innocent, urged on by fury and malice, so that the crime of murder remained. He thinks it implied that had they killed him knowing him to be the Messiah there would have been no forgiveness, and of the rulers he grants that their minds had been prejudiced by the expectation of a prince and a conqueror. On the prophecies Barnes is emphatic that the prediction changed nothing in the act, since foreknowledge does not take away guilt, and that Peter urges it not to acquit them but to show that, the death being part of a plan for opening pardon, there was mercy to be had; he calls it a signal instance of God overruling wicked conduct to his own purposes, while the sinner gets no credit from an outcome he never intended. Ellicott finds Peter's handling of ignorance in exact agreement with Paul's: men were ignorant where they might have known, had they not let prejudice overpower reason and conscience, so that their ignorance was not invincible and had to be repented of — yet because it was ignorance, repentance remained possible, and even the people and rulers of Israel came within the range of the prayer first offered for the Roman soldiers. Robertson sums it up in Hackett's phrase: they had sinned, but their sin was not of so deep a dye that it could not have been more heinous still.

debates.question: How far does the plea of ignorance carry?

positions.position: far enough to leave room for repentance, but not to innocence — the crime of murder remained, and had they known him to be the Messiah there would have been no forgiveness
far enough to keep them from despair, since a deed done in full knowledge would have been the least pardonable of sins
not simply, since hypocrisy lay hidden under it; the deed is named from error and blind zeal because those abounded, not because wickedness was absent

outliers.note: makes the ignorance culpable and useful at once — not invincible, so it must be repented of; but real, so that repentance is still open

themes: the turn from charge to appeal
what ignorance does and does not excuse

schools.summary: Gill notes that the Ethiopic version adds the words, and be baptized. Calvin observes that in exhorting to repentance Peter also declares that remission is prepared before the face of God, since no man can be stirred to repent unless salvation is set before him, and one who despairs of pardon, given over as it were to destruction already, does not fear to run headlong against God obstinately. This is why, he says, the Papists cannot deliver the doctrine of repentance: they babble much of it, but having overthrown the hope of grace they leave men's souls in doubt and fearfulness and cast them into a labyrinth, so that this part of the doctrine being corrupt they confound the rest also.

Henry states the necessity plainly, that the absolute necessity of repentance must be solemnly charged on the conscience of everyone who desires that his sins be blotted out and that he may share the refreshment which nothing but a sense of Christ's pardoning love can afford. He adds that it was not needful for the Holy Spirit to make known the times and seasons of these dispensations, which are still left obscure; but when sinners are convinced of their sins they will cry to the Lord for pardon, and to the penitent and believing the times of refreshment will come from the presence of the Lord.

Clarke reads the first word as a call to change the mind now that they are convinced this was the Messiah, and the second as turning to God through Christ, deeply deploring their transgressions and believing on his name. He connects the blotting out with the ceremony of the waters of jealousy, where the curse written in the book was blotted out with the bitter water, and presses it home: these men had said, his blood be upon us, so that their sins stood written against them and cried for punishment, and only that same blood could save them. On the times of refreshing he reports Lightfoot as contending that the clause should be rendered that the times of refreshing may come, and takes the word itself for a breathing time or respite, either the interval before the destruction of Jerusalem, given them to repent in, or the whole reign of the kingdom of grace with the peace, love and joy God gives to believers here below. Wesley glosses the second word as being turned from sin and Satan unto God, and makes the same complaint from the other end: the term, common as it is in modern writings, very rarely occurs in Scripture, and perhaps not once in the sense we now give it. Of the refreshing he adds that to others these times will assuredly come, whether these hearers repent or not.

Barnes complains that the English conveys an idea not in the original, that of passivity, as though the hearers were to yield to some outside influence; whereas the word means to turn, to return to a path one has strayed from, and then to turn away from sins. Repent and turn would be better, since being converted cannot well be made a matter of obligation, while turning to God is the duty of every sinner. Of the blotting out he takes the figure from creditors cancelling a debt, and more exactly from writing on tablets covered with wax and then inverting the stylus to smooth the wax again, so that every trace of the record disappears — which expresses forgiveness better than blotting does. Sin cannot be pardoned before a man repents of it, so that in the work of grace repentance always precedes pardon. On the disputed particle he lays out the two parties, Kuinoel, Grotius and the Syriac on one side, Calvin, Beza and the Vulgate on the other, and grants that the construction admits either; but he objects that it is hard to see how the repentance of these hearers should introduce the times of refreshing, and that this hardly suits a discourse meant to assure them that pardon might now be had. Ellicott is flattest: the conjunction never has the force of when, and the sense is, that so the times of refreshing may come — a thought found in both apostles, that the conversion of sinners, and of Israel especially, hastens the fulfilment of God's purposes. He takes the word for refreshing as unique in the New Testament, and distinguishes these seasons from the restitution that follows, calling them its gracious preludes, when the weary are quickened as by the fresh breeze of morning and the fire of persecution is assuaged; and he adds the sequel, that Israel as a nation did not repent, so that hatred and strife went on to the bitter end without refreshment. Robertson says flatly that it is not when, and that repentance surely brings seasons of refreshing from the presence of the Lord.

debates.question: Does the clause say the refreshing will come when they repent, or that it may come through their repenting?

positions.position: that so the times of refreshing may come — the conjunction never has the force of when
the construction admits either, but it is hard to see how their repenting could introduce the times of refreshing, and that reading hardly suits the design of the discourse

outliers.note: makes the offer of pardon a precondition of preaching repentance at all, since a man who despairs of it runs headlong against God rather than turning to him

schools.summary: Gill argues that neither coming will fit the sending meant here. It cannot be the first, since Christ had been sent and was gone again, which would leave the awakened hearers no hope after what they had done; and it cannot be the second, since they could only conclude he was coming to take vengeance and would look on him whom they had pierced with horror and trembling. What is meant is his being sent and coming in the ministration of the word and by his Spirit, to the comfort of their souls. Calvin makes the mention of judgment the engine of the exhortation. He prefers Beza's rendering to the elliptical construction of the older interpreters, and reads it thus: sins are forgiven against the day of the last judgment, since unless we are cited before God's judgment-seat we are not careful to pacify him. Nothing pricks men more than being taught that they must give an account, for while our senses are held fast in this world they lie drowned in a lethargy, and the message of the last judgment must sound like a trumpet before we are truly awake. He finds two spurs in it: the profit of faith does not appear in this world, where it often goes well with the despisers of God while the life of the godly is full of miseries, so that our hearts would faint if we did not remember a day of rest coming; and the fearful judgment shakes off delicacy besides. Peter therefore mixes threatenings with promises, partly to allure and partly to drive, and makes the day of Christ a thing his hearers may desire rather than dread — while saying expressly that Christ shall be the Judge, so that contempt of the gospel may be known to be punishable, which also comforts the faithful, since salvation lies in the hand of the one who now offers it. By adding that the Judge is he who is preached to them now, Peter takes away every excuse of ignorance.

Clarke lists the witnesses for the disputed reading — the chief uncials with fifty other copies, the Syriac, the Arabic and Chrysostom — and draws the point out of it: Christ crucified was the person God had from the beginning appointed for that people, so that what they were to expect was not a triumphant Messiah but one who must suffer and die; and by believing in him as thus suffering and dying for their sins, he would be sent again in the power of his Spirit to justify and save them. Wesley states his own reading briefly, that the apostles generally speak of the second coming as just at hand, and takes the appointment to have been made before the foundation of the world.

Barnes reports that a large majority of manuscripts read appointed where the received text reads preached, a reading approved by Griesbach, Knapp and Bengel and followed by the ancient Syriac, and he calls it undoubtedly the true one. He puts the whole under one economy: the Messiah is to be sent to teach, to redeem, to judge and to gather his people, which is itself the argument for repenting, that they might escape in the day of judgment. Ellicott gives the better reading in a line, which was fore-appointed for you, and renders the opening clause as before, and that he may send. Robertson agrees on the text, deriving the word from a root meaning ready to hand, so that it carries the sense of choosing; and he notes that the order is not Jesus Christ nor Christ Jesus but the Messiah, Jesus, which identifies the one with the other. Of the sending he takes the reference to be naturally to the second coming, as the next verse shows, though he allows with Knowling a spiritual presence of the enthroned Jesus which believers enjoy as a foretaste, and that repentance helps get the world ready for the King.

positions.position: neither the first coming nor the second, but a coming in the ministration of the word and by his Spirit, to the comfort of their souls
a sending again in the power of his Spirit, on their believing in him as one who suffered and died for their sins
the second coming, as the following verse shows, though a spiritual presence is enjoyed meanwhile as a foretaste

outliers.note: reads the whole verse as a summons to the judgment-seat, on the ground that men are not careful to pacify God until they are cited to appear before him

themes: the day of judgment as motive

schools.summary: Gill takes the clause either way — heaven holds and retains him in his human nature, which does not at all hinder his coming meanwhile to his people in a spiritual way, to their joy and comfort, or else he must receive heaven, the kingdom and the glory, and reign there. Calvin notices the same ambiguity and refuses to settle it: the words may mean that Christ is comprehended in the heavens or that he comprehends them, and since the expression is doubtful we should hold to what is certain, that Christ is to be sought nowhere but in heaven while we hope for the last restoring of all things. Men's senses being always bent toward a gross and earthly beholding of God, these hearers might have believed him risen without knowing where he was; Peter prevents them by saying he is in heaven, so that they may lift their minds on high and seek him with the eyes of faith, however far he is from them. Calvin then distinguishes force from effect: Christ has already restored all things by his death, but the effect does not yet appear, the restoring being still in course while we groan under the burden of servitude, the kingdom only begun and its perfection deferred to the last day. If we see much confusion in the world, this hope should set us on our feet; Christ does not appear at once because the warfare of the Church is not yet complete, its term appointed by God and not ours to anticipate. He also finds in the appeal to all the prophets a mark of true antiquity, since God himself is the author, the holy prophets the witnesses, and the continual course of times confirms the testimony — a confirmation especially necessary for men brought up in the doctrine of the law, who ought to admit nothing that does not agree with it.

Clarke says that Christ has already appeared on earth and accomplished the end of his appearing, has ascended to administer the concerns of his kingdom, and will continue there till he comes to judge the quick and the dead. On the restitution he gets the sense from the prefix, which implies that the good state now settled was preceded by a bad one, as when the disciples asked whether he would restore the kingdom to Israel and meant, take it from the Romans and give it back; connected here with what the prophets have spoken, it must mean the accomplishment of all the promises relative to the kingdom of Christ, the whole reign of grace, whose energetic influence destroys the bad state and establishes the good. This is done in every believing soul, all things being restored to their primitive order; and when such a work becomes universal, then all things will be restored in the fullest sense. He notes that the word all is absent from the chief manuscripts, and offers two readings of the last phrase — from the giving of the law, or from the foundation of the world. Wesley reads the phrase as comprising the whole course of New Testament times between the ascension and the coming in glory, the most eminent being the apostolic age and the spotless Church, which will consist of all the Jews and Gentiles united after all persecutions and apostasies are at an end.

Barnes explains why the ascension needed establishing: the common Jewish belief was that the Messiah would reign on earth for ever, so his absence was an objection against him, and the apostles had to establish the ascension, their evidence being that they had watched it. The word rendered must means that it was fit or proper, that he might direct the affairs of the universe for the church and exercise there his office of intercession; and Barnes thinks it remarkable that Peter cited no text for it. On the restitution he takes the verb from its use for restoring a sprained limb, notes its use in Josephus for the return from Babylon, and presses a second sense found in Philo, that of consummation or filling up, which the Syriac and Arabic versions adopt: until the complement of the times, that is, of all that the prophets foretold. He is careful about the limit: all things means all the prophets spoke, and does not mean that all men shall be saved or that every evil of sin can be repaired — the mischief is done and cannot be undone. Ellicott gives the verb a pregnant force: receive and hold. He prefers restoration to an earlier and better state over simple consummation, finds a parallel in the promise of new heavens and a new earth, denies that the word necessarily involves the salvation of all men, and yet holds that it expresses a state in which righteousness rather than sin has dominion — which suggests a wider hope of growth in holiness, or even of repentance, in the unseen world than Christendom has been content with. He finds in the clause about the prophets a compact statement of doctrine: they spoke as they were moved, and he who spoke by them was nothing less than God. Robertson adds that the papyri use it for repairs to temples, and that as a medical term it means restoration to health.

debates.question: Does the word mean restoring an earlier state, or completing a foretold one?

positions.position: consummation or filling up — until the complement of the times, that is, of all the prophets foretold, and not the salvation of all men
restoration to an earlier and better state, in which righteousness rather than sin has dominion, which suggests a wider hope than Christendom has been content with

outliers.note: explains the delay by the Church's unfinished warfare, whose term God has appointed and we may not anticipate — the restoring is real but still in course

themes: received by heaven, or receiving it

schools.summary: Cyril takes the passage as a question of chronology rather than of likeness, reserving the phrase about being like Moses to be examined in its proper place and asking instead when this expected prophet came. He answers from Jacob's blessing on Judah, that a prince shall not fail out of Judah nor a ruler from his loins until he come for whom it is reserved, who is the expectation not of the Jews but of the Gentiles; the cessation of the Jewish rule was therefore given as the sign of Christ's advent.

Gill notes that the phrase about the fathers means the Israelites in the times of Moses, that the Ethiopic version reads our fathers, and that the words are absent from the Latin and Syriac versions and the Alexandrian copy. Calvin makes the same defence of the citation that Barnes does from the other side, that Peter thereby proves he is not making them revolt from Moses, since obeying this chief teacher is itself part of the law. He grants that plainer testimonies lay to hand, and explains the choice: what is in question is the authority of the teaching, and Peter would have preached all else in vain unless they were first persuaded that this teacher must be reverently heard. On the harder question Calvin argues at greater length and will go no further than the text allows. The context shows that Moses does not speak of one man only, since after forbidding the people to turn aside to enchanters and soothsayers he shows them a remedy, promising that God will be careful at all times to send them prophets; those who catch at the phrase about likeness press it too hard, and there is no cause why we should be laughed at by the Jews for wresting the words, as if Moses spoke of Christ alone. Yet the citation is fit, since what appertains to the other prophets chiefly commends Christ, the one toward whom every former prophecy was directed, and by whose mouth God at last spoke absolutely; and it came to pass that prophets were wanting for some ages before his coming, as may be gathered from Malachi, who passes from the law straight to the Baptist and to Christ.
Henry calls it a powerful stroke to warn them of unbelief in the words of their favourite prophet, out of pretended zeal for whom they were ready to reject Christianity.

Clarke draws it further: Christ came not as an ordinary prophet exhorting to repentance and amendment but as a legislator giving a new law, whose commands and precepts they were to obey on pain of endless destruction, so that the gospel supersedes the old. Wesley sets out the likeness in particulars: Moses instituted the Jewish Church and Christ the Christian; with the prophesying of Moses was joined the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, and with Christ's the deliverance of his people from sin and death; those who could not bear the voice of God yet desired to hear Moses, and much more do men wearied with the law desire to hear Christ; Moses spoke only what God commanded, and so did Christ — yet though like Moses he was infinitely superior in person and office.

Barnes answers from the aim of the sermon: the authority of Moses was absolute, so it mattered to show that they were not departing from his law but that he had foretold this; and since Peter's object was to fix their guilt, he sets their obligation to obey before them by the command that whoever would not hear such a prophet should be cut off — so that in putting him to death they violated their own lawgiver. He reads the passage in its context, where Moses warns the people against the enchanters of surrounding nations and assures them that the Lord will raise up a prophet from time to time to guide them instead; so understood, the promise pertains to the series of prophets and has no direct reference to the Messiah, except as he was one of that series. Peter's appeal rests on the Messiah sustaining the character of a prophet, on the words applying to him by eminence, and on this being such an emergency as the promise contemplated; and Barnes adds that the Jews were accustomed to apply the name prophet to the Messiah, and that their own rabbins held he would be the greatest of the prophets, greater even than Moses. Ellicott admits the earlier prophets as partial fulfilments, while observing that the words had fixed men's minds on one great prophet excelling all others, as the question put to the Baptist shows; none between Moses and Jesus had marked a new epoch, been the channel of a new revelation, or given a new law. He notices that the clause about hearing him in all things is a parenthesis, suggesting a quotation from memory. Robertson notes that Moses claims to have been raised up a prophet himself, and that a greater would follow.

debates.question: Does the promise in Deuteronomy speak of one prophet or of many?

positions.position: of the series of prophets, with no direct reference to the Messiah except as one of that series; Peter's appeal rests on eminence, not on exclusive prediction
of the series, admitted as partial fulfilments, but the words had rightly fixed men's minds on one great prophet excelling all others
of the Messiah, Moses claiming that a greater than himself would come

outliers.note: refuses to press the likeness onto Christ alone, warning that wresting the words would only earn the scorn of Jewish readers — the citation is fit without it, since every former prophecy was directed toward Christ

themes: why Moses rather than a plainer prophecy

23.pericope_label: The threat, and the witnesses from Samuel

schools.summary: Gill glosses the subject simply as every person, man or woman, and on the roll of witnesses adds the Jewish titles for Samuel, master of the prophets and first in the chain of tradition; he observes that few prophets stood between him and Moses where many followed after, the schools having been set up in his days, and that a famous prophecy concerning Christ stands in the books that bear his name. Calvin makes the penalty establish the authority of the teaching. The authority of all the prophets, and most of all of Christ, is settled by this grievous punishment of the rebellious, and for good reason: since God accounts nothing more precious than his word, he cannot suffer it to be contemned, and under the law a man who despised it was adjudged to die. He reads the phrase about being put away from among the people against the adoption of Abraham's stock, made on the terms that simply to be numbered among them should be their chief felicity — blessed is the people whose God is the Lord. It follows that whoever refuses to hear Christ is blotted out of the book of life, since no man is worthy to be counted of the Church who refuses the Master by whom God teaches, and a man who will not be under the Head cuts himself off from the body. Of the prophets Calvin adds that they all with one consent send their scholars to Christ, which makes much for the certainty of the gospel, since teachers spread over a long series of ages so temper their doctrine that they testify together that men should hope for a better and more perfect thing — so that whoever will believe Moses and the prophets must submit to the doctrine of Christ, without which all they taught is lame and imperfect.

Clarke reports Lightfoot on the pairing of the two names, that Moses and Samuel are coupled here as in the Psalm because there were few or no prophets between them, the appearance of angels having been commoner, and that after the death of Phinehas it is doubtful whether the oracle by Urim and Thummim continued till Samuel's time, when prophecy revived; he adds the Jewish saying that Samuel was the chief of the prophets, and thinks Peter may have had it in view. Wesley admires the construction of the appeal: one cannot imagine a more masterly warning to the Jews of the consequence of their unbelief, made in the very words of their favourite prophet, out of a pretended zeal for whom they had rejected Christ.

Barnes points out that the verb here is not the usual one for coming to pass but carries the sense of obligation, and that the sentence gives the meaning of the older passage rather than its letter: the Hebrew reads that God will require it of the man, which the Greek version turns into taking vengeance, without specifying how. The customary mode of punishing such offences was cutting the offender off from among the people, and though the word chosen here properly means to exterminate, to be destroyed from among a people meant excommunication — the loss of sacrifice, of worship, of standing, so that a man was reckoned a heathen and an outcast, which was probably the severest penalty the nation knew. He turns it on the hearers, that in crucifying Jesus they had exposed themselves to the severest punishment their law knew, and had all the more reason to repent. Of Samuel he supposes he is named because he was the first prophet after Moses to record a prediction touching the Messiah, since the Jews counted Joshua the first of the prophets but neither Joshua nor Judges contains a distinct one; from Moses to Samuel probably no prophet arose, God being consulted instead by Urim and Thummim. Ellicott agrees that the substituted words echo a phrase familiar from Exodus and Leviticus, and takes this for another free citation; of Samuel he gives both reasons, that he founded those schools and so represents the whole goodly fellowship, and that he uttered one of the earliest predictions reckoned distinctively Messianic. Robertson notes the emphatic form of that prophet and the symmetry behind it, that the people had refused to hearken to Moses and many were now refusing to hearken to Christ; the verb for destroying utterly is late, found here alone in the New Testament though common in the Greek Old Testament, and schools of prophets arose in Samuel's time where few had been before.

outliers.note: reads the threatened excision as an argument about church membership: a man who refuses the one Master by whom God teaches has cut himself off from the body, not merely incurred a penalty

themes: what being destroyed from the people meant
why the roll begins at Samuel

25.pericope_label: Sons of the prophets and of the covenant

schools.summary: Gill takes the title of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who are called prophets, and holds that these hearers were lineally and naturally descended from them, so that the prophecies of the Old Testament concerning the Messiah and the promises of him belonged to them, and they were heirs of them. Calvin builds a doctrine of the covenanted family on the verse. The grace of the covenant, he says, was appointed principally for these hearers, and Peter, having pricked them forward with the terror of punishment, now allures them with the grace offered in Christ — it being a wise minister's duty to prick forward the sluggish and lead gently those apt to be taught. He presses the necessity of that particular application: it is not enough that mercy be preached generally, since a man who thought the gospel had come by chance would have a wavering opinion instead of faith, and God does not cast forth uncertain voices to hang in the air but directs them to us by his determinate counsel. The argument itself he states as a syllogism — God made his covenant with our fathers, therefore we their posterity are comprehended in it — and turns it against those who expound the children of Abraham only allegorically, as though God had no respect to the stock when he promised to be the God of Abraham's seed. Peter is not speaking of the shadows of the law, Calvin insists, but affirming that under the kingdom of Christ God adopts the children with the fathers, so that the grace of salvation reaches those not yet born. He grants the objection, that many children of the faithful according to the flesh are counted bastards, having thrust themselves out of the holy progeny by unbelief; but this does not hinder the Lord from admitting the seed of the godly into the fellowship of grace, and though the common election is not effectual in all, it may set open a gate for the special elect.

Clarke makes the phrase an argument aimed at the men themselves: as children or disciples of the prophets they were bound to believe their predictions and obey their precepts, and were entitled to their promises, so that duty and interest went hand in hand and there is not a blessing contained in the covenant made with their fathers but belongs to them — and since that covenant respected the blessings of the gospel, they must believe in Jesus Christ to be put in possession of them. Wesley says the same in a line, that as the first heirs the prophecies and the covenant belong to them properly.

Barnes takes the first title as discipleship rather than descent: they were not the literal posterity of the prophets but their pupils, since teachers among the Jews were commonly called fathers and their disciples sons — and as professed disciples they were bound to listen, and as men living among the people to whom the promises were made they should embrace the Messiah. On the second title he supplies a careful definition. A covenant properly means a compact between parties who have a right to choose or refuse the terms; applied to God and man it means a firm promise on God's part, to be regarded with all the sacredness of a compact, and is called a covenant only to mark that sacredness and the certainty of its fulfilment — for since man has no right to reject any of the terms, there has strictly been no compact between them at all. He adds that the word rendered kindreds means those who have a common father or ancestor, applied to families and then to whole nations, and plainly means all nations here; and that the promise about the seed, as Paul affirms, had express reference to the Messiah. Ellicott finds in the choice of the Abrahamic covenant a mark of the unity of apostolic teaching, since Peter rests on it with as full an emphasis as Paul does after learning that it implicitly involved the calling of the Gentiles. Robertson notes the emphatic pronoun and the figure of the Greek, literally the covenant which God covenanted, the noun and the verb being of one root; the covenant was made with Abraham and repeated at various times, and in the letter to the Hebrews the same word does duty for covenant and for will.

debates.question: In what sense were the hearers sons of the prophets?

positions.position: as disciples and pupils, teachers being called fathers among the Jews and their followers sons
as lineal and natural descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and so heirs of the promises made to them

outliers.note: denies that there has strictly been any compact between God and man at all, since a party with no right to refuse the terms cannot contract — the word covenant marks the sacredness of the promise, not its form

themes: sons by descent or by discipleship
what a covenant with God can mean
the children comprehended with the fathers

26.pericope_label: Unto you first, to bless you

schools.summary: Gill allows either reading of the raising up, since the phrase is sometimes used of the incarnation and the manifestation of Christ in human nature, and sometimes of the resurrection and the exaltation at God's right hand. Calvin gathers from the words of Moses that Christ is now revealed, reasoning that the blessing could not otherwise be, unless the beginning of it flowed from the Messiah: all mankind being accursed, a singular remedy is promised which Christ alone performs, so that he is the only fountain and beginning of the blessing — and if he came to bless the Jews first and us afterwards, he has done what was his to do, and we shall feel the force of it in ourselves unless our unbelief hinder. He notes that blessing the people was part of the priest's office under the law, with a promise added lest it be a vain ceremony, and that what was shadowed in the old priesthood was truly performed in Christ. He declines the rendering of Erasmus, which speaks of a thing done long ago, and holds instead that Christ was raised up when he was declared to be the author of the blessing — a thing done lately and suddenly, which ought to have moved these hearers the more. To raise up a prophet, he explains, is to furnish him with the gifts his office needs and prefer him to the degree of prophetical honour; Christ was so raised when he fulfilled the function his Father enjoined, and the same is done daily whenever he is offered in the gospel. Calvin closes on the order of benefits: Christ does not do away the sins of the faithful so that they may take licence to sin under that colour, but makes them new men at the same time, as Isaiah promises a Redeemer to Zion and then adds the reservation, to those in Jacob who turn from their iniquities.

Clarke ties the verse to the previous one, that as children of the prophets and of the covenant the first offers of salvation belonged to them by right, and that the great mission of Christ is directed first to them, that they may be saved from their sins. He draws two conclusions and presses them hard. The salvation promised in the covenant was from sin and not from the Romans, and no man has his sin blotted out who does not turn from it; and neither political nor ecclesiastical privilege benefits the soul by itself, since a man may have Abraham for his father according to the flesh and Satan for his father according to the spirit — for if he is not turned from his iniquities, even the death of Christ profits him nothing. He adds a question for the reader, whether it is not the duty and interest of every Christian, in reading the Scriptures, to search for the testimony they bear to Christ and the salvation procured by his death. Wesley closes the chapter by calling this the great gospel blessing, that we are blessed by being turned from our iniquities.

Barnes takes it for the rule that the gospel should be preached to the Jews before others, beginning at Jerusalem, and notes that Jesus himself had confined his ministry to them. He denies that the raising up refers to the resurrection, taking it in the sense the words of Moses had borne, where God promised to raise up a prophet and send him — so that Peter means God had commissioned his Son to preach and turn men from their sins. Of the blessing he says the highest that can be conferred on men is to be turned from sin, the source of all their woes, and that Christ blesses nobody in sin but only by turning him out of it; the design of Peter's remarks was to show that the Messiah had come and that they might now look for happiness, pardon and mercy through him, and what was true for the Jews is true for all. Ellicott hears in the turn of the phrase an agreement with Paul's formula about the Jew first and also the Gentile, and draws an inference: Peter does not yet know on what conditions the gospel will be preached to the heathen, but the word implies a distinct perception that there was a call to preach to them at all. He renders the second title as Servant, as before, and notes a nicety of the Greek, that the participle is present where the English gives an infinitive, so that Christ is sent as in the act of blessing. The verb which commonly means a spoken benediction is here used for the reality of blessedness, and the blessing is found not in exemption from punishment, nor even in pardon and reconciliation, but in a change of heart, in turning each man from his wickednesses — the plural implying all the concrete forms in which man's wickedness could show itself. Robertson puts the reason for the order in a sentence: the Jews were first in privilege, and through them the Messiah was to come for all the families of the earth.

debates.question: What does having raised up his Servant refer to?

positions.position: not the resurrection, but the commissioning promised in Moses, where God said he would raise up a prophet and send him
either the incarnation and manifestation in the flesh, or the resurrection and exaltation
the declaring of Christ as author of the blessing — a furnishing for office, done lately and suddenly, and done daily whenever he is offered in the gospel

outliers.note: cuts off two false securities at once, since a man may have Abraham for his father according to the flesh and Satan according to the spirit, and may belong to the visible Church with no title to the Church triumphant
